blocks.raw: # Organizing Dataflows using Applications
blocks.text: Organizing Dataflows using Applications

blocks.raw: The Applications feature in Neo provides a structured way to organize and manage dataflows within an organization. The feature helps group related dataflows under a logical container based on their purpose or business function.
blocks.text: The Applications feature in Neo provides a structured way to organize and manage dataflows within an organization. The feature helps group related dataflows under a logical container based on their purpose or business function.

blocks.raw: For example, you can create an application named Customer Management and group all dataflows that create, update, or validate customer profiles under that application. This helps keep similar dataflows organized in one place, making it easier to locate, maintain, and track them as the number of dataflows increases in your organization.
blocks.text: For example, you can create an application named Customer Management and group all dataflows that create, update, or validate customer profiles under that application. This helps keep similar dataflows organized in one place, making it easier to locate, maintain, and track them as the number of dataflows increases in your organization.

blocks.raw: # Types of applications
blocks.text: Types of applications

blocks.raw: To support different kinds of dataflow grouping, Neo provides three application types. An application type defines how Neo classifies and manages dataflows within an application. Each application type serves a different purpose and follows specific management rules within Neo. The following are the application types:
blocks.text: To support different kinds of dataflow grouping, Neo provides three application types. An application type defines how Neo classifies and manages dataflows within an application. Each application type serves a different purpose and follows specific management rules within Neo. The following are the application types:

blocks.raw:
* Default Application

* Middleware Application

* Custom Applications
blocks.text: Default ApplicationMiddleware ApplicationCustom Applications

blocks.raw: The following sections describe each application type and how Neo manages dataflows within them.
blocks.text: The following sections describe each application type and how Neo manages dataflows within them.

blocks.raw: ## Default application
blocks.text: Default application

blocks.raw: The Default Application is available by default and contains all existing dataflows created before the Applications feature was introduced.
blocks.text: The Default Application is available by default and contains all existing dataflows created before the Applications feature was introduced.

blocks.raw: **Key behaviors**
blocks.text: Key behaviors

blocks.raw:
* Adds new dataflows to the Default Application unless you select a different application.

* Allows moving dataflows from the Default Application to a custom application.

* Does not allow moving dataflows back to the Default Application.
blocks.text: Adds new dataflows to the Default Application unless you select a different application.Allows moving dataflows from the Default Application to a custom application.Does not allow moving dataflows back to the Default Application.

blocks.raw: ## Middleware application
blocks.text: Middleware application

blocks.raw: The Middleware Application is a system-managed application that automatically groups dataflows based on [tags](https://docs.capillarytech.com/docs/tags-filters-in-dataflow#/). You cannot manually add, edit, or move dataflows in or out of this application.
blocks.text: The Middleware Application is a system-managed application that automatically groups dataflows based on tags. You cannot manually add, edit, or move dataflows in or out of this application.

blocks.raw: Middleware dataflows are identified by the following tags:
blocks.text: Middleware dataflows are identified by the following tags:

blocks.raw:
* Pre-matching

* Post-matching
blocks.text: Pre-matchingPost-matching

blocks.raw: These tags determine when the dataflow runs in relation to the main dataflow execution.
blocks.text: These tags determine when the dataflow runs in relation to the main dataflow execution.

blocks.raw: **Key behaviors**
blocks.text: Key behaviors

blocks.raw:
* Moves the dataflow to the Middleware Application when you assign a pre-matching or post-matching tag.

* Moves the dataflow to the Default Application when you remove the tag.

* Prevents manually moving dataflows into or out of the Middleware Application.

* Prevents moving middleware dataflows to custom applications unless the matching tag is removed.

blocks.raw: ## Custom application
blocks.text: Custom application

blocks.raw: Custom applications group dataflows based on specific business functions or use cases.
blocks.text: Custom applications group dataflows based on specific business functions or use cases.

blocks.raw: **Key behaviors**
blocks.text: Key behaviors

blocks.raw:
* Allows creating custom applications if you have the Neo Edit permission.

* Allows moving dataflows from the Default Application to a custom application.

* Allows moving dataflows between custom applications.

* Allows renaming custom applications from the UI.

blocks.raw: Once you determine how you want to group your dataflows, you can create a custom application for each group. The section below explains how to create a custom application.

blocks.raw: # Application context in dataflow execution
blocks.text: Application context in dataflow execution

blocks.raw: Neo makes the application context available during the execution of each dataflow. This means you can write conditional logic inside a dataflow based on the application it belongs to.
blocks.text: Neo makes the application context available during the execution of each dataflow. This means you can write conditional logic inside a dataflow based on the application it belongs to.

blocks.raw: For middleware dataflows, the application context refers to the application of the main dataflow that triggered the middleware — not the middleware's own application. This is enabled through the DAO function [getApplicationName](https://docs.capillarytech.com/docs/neo-dao-functions#getapplicationname).
blocks.text: For middleware dataflows, the application context refers to the application of the main dataflow that triggered the middleware — not the middleware's own application. This is enabled through the DAO function getApplicationName.

blocks.raw: ## Using `getApplicationName` in middleware dataflows
blocks.text: Using getApplicationName in middleware dataflows

blocks.raw: Middleware dataflows (pre-matching and post-matching filters) run before or after every main dataflow in your organization. In some cases, you may want a middleware to apply its logic only for dataflows that belong to a specific application, and skip execution for others.
blocks.text: Middleware dataflows (pre-matching and post-matching filters) run before or after every main dataflow in your organization. In some cases, you may want a middleware to apply its logic only for dataflows that belong to a specific application, and skip execution for others.

blocks.raw: The `getApplicationName` function lets you identify the calling application at runtime and use that information to control the execution path.
blocks.text: The getApplicationName function lets you identify the calling application at runtime and use that information to control the execution path.

blocks.raw: **Key behaviors**
blocks.text: Key behaviors

blocks.raw:
* Returns the application name of the calling main dataflow when invoked from within a middleware dataflow.
* Returns the application name of the current dataflow when invoked from within a main dataflow.
* Is available in Script blocks, Schema blocks, and relation conditions.
blocks.text: Returns the application name of the calling main dataflow when invoked from within a middleware dataflow.Returns the application name of the current dataflow when invoked from within a main dataflow.Is available in Script blocks, Schema blocks, and relation conditions.

blocks.raw: ### Use case: Run middleware only for specific applications
blocks.text: Use case: Run middleware only for specific applications

blocks.raw: **Requirement**
blocks.text: Requirement

blocks.raw: Your organization has a pre-matching middleware dataflow that performs an authentication step. You want this middleware to execute its full logic only for dataflows inside the `CustomerManagement` application, and return early for all others.
blocks.text: Your organization has a pre-matching middleware dataflow that performs an authentication step. You want this middleware to execute its full logic only for dataflows inside the CustomerManagement application, and return early for all others.

blocks.raw: **Solution**
blocks.text: Solution

blocks.raw: Add a Script block named `ValidateApplication` at the start of the middleware dataflow. This block uses `getApplicationName` to identify the calling application and checks it against a list of applications that should run the middleware. A relation condition then routes execution based on that check.
blocks.text: Add a Script block named ValidateApplication at the start of the middleware dataflow. This block uses getApplicationName to identify the calling application and checks it against a list of applications that should run the middleware. A relation condition then routes execution based on that check.

blocks.raw: **Step 1: Add a `ValidateApplication` Script block**
blocks.text: Step 1: Add a ValidateApplication Script block

blocks.raw: **Step 2: Configure a relation on the `ValidateApplication` block**
blocks.text: Step 2: Configure a relation on the ValidateApplication block

blocks.raw: In the **Relations** section of the `ValidateApplication` block, add the following path relation:
blocks.text: In the Relations section of the ValidateApplication block, add the following path relation:

blocks.raw:
```javascript
dao.getBody("ValidateApplication").allowedApplications.includes(
  dao.getBody("ValidateApplication").currentApplication
)
```

* If this evaluates to `true`, execution proceeds to the main middleware logic block.
* If this evaluates to `false`, execution routes to an exit block, skipping the middleware logic.
blocks.text: If this evaluates to true, execution proceeds to the main middleware logic block.If this evaluates to false, execution routes to an exit block, skipping the middleware logic.

blocks.raw: ### Use case: Route to different logic per application within the same middleware
blocks.text: Use case: Route to different logic per application within the same middleware

blocks.raw: If your organization requires different middleware logic for different applications, you can handle multiple applications within a single middleware dataflow. This is useful when you have reached the limit of pre-matching or post-matching filter slots (maximum three each).
blocks.text: If your organization requires different middleware logic for different applications, you can handle multiple applications within a single middleware dataflow. This is useful when you have reached the limit of pre-matching or post-matching filter slots (maximum three each).

blocks.raw: **Step 1: Add a `RouteApplication` Script block**
blocks.text: Step 1: Add a RouteApplication Script block

blocks.raw: **Step 2: Define multiple relations on the `RouteApplication` block**
blocks.text: Step 2: Define multiple relations on the RouteApplication block

blocks.raw:
* **Relation 1:** `dao.getBody("RouteApplication").allowedApplicationsSet1.includes(dao.getBody("RouteApplication").currentApplication)` — connects to the `LogicForCustomerManagement` block.
* **Relation 2:** `dao.getBody("RouteApplication").allowedApplicationsSet2.includes(dao.getBody("RouteApplication").currentApplication)` — connects to the `LogicForOrderTracking` block.
blocks.text: Relation 1: dao.getBody("RouteApplication").allowedApplicationsSet1.includes(dao.getBody("RouteApplication").currentApplication) — connects to the LogicForCustomerManagement block.Relation 2: dao.getBody("RouteApplication").allowedApplicationsSet2.includes(dao.getBody("RouteApplication").currentApplication) — connects to the LogicForOrderTracking block.

blocks.raw: A single middleware dataflow can now serve multiple applications with distinct logic.

blocks.raw: # FAQs
blocks.text: FAQs

blocks.raw:
1. What is the purpose of Applications in Neo?\
   Applications help you organize related dataflows under logical containers so you can manage, view, and maintain them more easily.
2. Can I create a new application?\
   Yes. You can create custom applications if you have the Neo Edit permission.
3. How many custom applications can I create?\
   You can create up to 20 custom applications in an organization.
4. Can I rename an application?\
   Yes. You can rename custom applications if you have the Neo Edit permission.
5. Can I delete an application?\
   No. Applications cannot be deleted from the UI.
6. Can I move dataflows between applications?\
   Yes. You can move dataflows between custom applications or from the Default Application to a custom application. You must have the Neo Edit permission.
7. Can I move dataflows into the Middleware Application?\
   No. Dataflows are moved into the Middleware Application automatically based on pre-matching or post-matching tags.
8. What happens if I remove a pre-matching or post-matching tag from a middleware dataflow?\
   The dataflow automatically moves to the Default Application.
9. Do tags affect where dataflows appear?\
   Only matching-related tags (pre-matching and post-matching) affect placement. All other tags are informational and do not control where dataflows are grouped.
10. Does moving a dataflow change its execution URL or behavior?\
    No. Application grouping affects only how dataflows are organized in the UI. It does not change the execution URL, logic, or behavior.
11. Can I view applications without edit permissions?\
    Yes. Users with the Neo Viewer permission can view all applications and their dataflows.
12. Are applications available for global dataflows?\
    Yes. Applications are visible for global dataflows, but you cannot create or modify global applications from the UI.
